strengths: Novel and simple optical design that exploits natural chromatic aberration with off-the-shelf lenses, achieving high light efficiency and low hardware complexity (4 optical components).
Fast reconstruction algorithm (0.64s) via efficient matrix inversion and plug-and-play ADMM, with a well-motivated physics-based forward model.
Competitive performance on synthetic benchmarks: highest PSNR (24.10 dB) and SSIM (0.61) among compared methods, with good spectral reconstruction and minimal hallucination artifacts.
Real prototype built and evaluated on a Macbeth color checker with quantitative metrics (SAM, ΔE00) and robustness analysis across distances and number of measurements.
Code and data publicly available on GitHub, supporting reproducibility.
Clear and well-written paper with thorough related work and a convincing proof-of-concept.
weaknesses: Limited real-world evaluation: only a few scenes and a color checker, with visible artifacts that require additional measurements (6) to resolve; spectral accuracy on real data is moderate (average ΔE00 3.77, SAM up to 38.0).

Method requires multiple exposures (5 for hyperspectral, >3 for RGB), so it is not single-shot; the absolute frame rate in simulation is low (0.21 fps), making the 'fast' claim relative to other methods rather than absolute.

Reliance on an off-the-shelf deep denoiser and a low-rank spectral prior from external datasets makes the algorithm hybrid rather than purely physics-based, slightly contradicting the 'interpretable physics-based' claim.

Comparison with other methods may not be entirely fair due to simulation assumptions (e.g., ideal camera, perfect alignment) and limited baselines; no comparison with recent deep learning-based spectral imaging methods.
Assumes static scenes and a specific depth range; performance degrades outside the working volume, and dynamic scenes are not addressed (acknowledged as future work).
The 'state-of-the-art' claim is not consistent across all metrics (SAM is worse than KRISM).

strengths: Simple, low-cost, light-efficient hardware: two off-the-shelf lenses plus a grayscale sensor with no coded aperture, disperser, or filter array, preserving photon throughput and using only 4 optical components versus up to 20 for KRISM. This is a genuinely attractive practical profile for low-cost hyperspectral imaging.

A complete and internally coherent computational pipeline: measured PSF calibration across 12 wavelengths and 12 lens positions, an explicit convolutional forward model, a spectral PCA prior, plug-and-play ADMM, and a BCCB-based fast matrix inversion that brings reconstruction down to 0.64 s.

Quantitatively strong PSNR on the simulated Harvard benchmark (24.10 dB vs. MST 21.18, KRISM 21.12, Choi et al. 15.97, SDC 12.03, Zhan et al. 6.11), with second-best SSIM (0.61) and SAM (36.51) against six baselines spanning spectral-filter, dispersive-element, and chromatic-aberration categories.

A working real-world prototype with quantitative perceptual evaluation (Macbeth chart, ΔE00 per patch, SAM on selected patches) plus useful robustness studies over working distance (Fig. 5a) and number of measurements (Fig. 5b), which characterize how the system degrades outside its calibration assumptions.
Demonstration of a genuine hyperspectral advantage over RGB: the metameric food-item pixels (points 5 and 6 in Fig. 3) that MST and RGB cannot separate are resolved by the proposed method.
Public release of code and data is promised, which is valuable for a hardware-plus-algorithm system paper.
weaknesses: The headline 'fast' / 'high frame rate' claim is not adequately supported and the temporal comparison is internally inconsistent. The abstract's '<1 second' refers only to compute (0.64 s), while the simulation grants every method a 5 s total exposure, so acquisition time is equalized and carries no information. Moreover, the frame-rate axis in Fig. 1(a) is not reconcilable with the caption's stated 5 s total exposure: SDC is plotted near 0.02 fps (implying ~50 s) and KRISM is plotted at ~0.21 fps, i.e. above 'Ours' at ~0.19 fps. Lens translation time and mechanical settling for the moving lens are also excluded from the 0.64 s figure. As presented, the speed claim, which is one of the three listed contributions, is not evidenced.

The 'state-of-the-art spectral image quality' claim holds for PSNR but not for spectral fidelity. SAM = 36.51° is worse than KRISM's 34.38°, and a spectral angle of ~36° is poor for the material-identification and food-quality applications the paper motivates. PSNR in hyperspectral reconstruction is largely dominated by spatial fidelity, so it is a weak proxy for spectral accuracy. On real data the reported SAM for the three RGB patches is 7.6°, 12.0°, and 38.0°, and the mean ΔE00 over the Macbeth chart is 3.77, above the value of 2 that the paper itself calls perceptually equivalent.

Evaluation breadth and statistical rigor are limited. The main comparison is a single simulated configuration over 30 Harvard images, with no variance, error bars, or per-image breakdown; only five images appear in Fig. 3. There is no ablation on the number of principal components, the choice of denoiser, or the number of measurements beyond the single curve in Fig. 5b. The image size/resolution used for the 0.64 s timing on an A6000 is not reported, so scalability is unclear. Real-data evaluation is confined to a color chart and a few lab scenes with no ground-truth spectra for natural scenes.

Fairness of the baseline comparison is uncertain. All baselines are re-simulated under a common 5 s exposure with added optical blocking effects and ideal-camera assumptions (zero read noise, no quantization, no transition time), rather than compared against their reported numbers. MST is additionally handicapped because its training data spans only 453-648 nm, which the authors acknowledge. The TF baseline at -4.88 dB PSNR and 88.71° SAM is implausible for a tuned method and suggests weak baseline configuration, which would inflate the reported margin.

The practical spectral resolution is low and the band count is ambiguous. PSFs are calibrated at 12 visible bandpass filters (400-694 nm), which limits the effective dimensionality to roughly 12 channels, yet the method is described as reconstructing a 'high dimensional spectrum' and is evaluated on the Harvard dataset with an unspecified C. The relationship between the 12-band calibration and the C channels used in evaluation/reconstruction is not stated, which undermines both the 'hyperspectral' framing and reproducibility.

Novelty is incremental relative to existing chromatic-aberration and focal-stack spectral imaging work ([10], [17], [31], [32], and [7] are all cited and closely related). The technical contribution here is largely the integration of existing ingredients: a moving-lens chromatic focal sweep, a PCA spectral subspace learned from the Harvard dataset, plug-and-play ADMM with an off-the-shelf denoiser, and a BCCB inversion trick.

The 'physics-based, interpretable, hallucination-mitigating' framing is in tension with the method itself. The reconstruction depends on a PCA basis learned from external spectral data and on a learned denoiser, and hallucination is asserted rather than measured (no hallucination metric or out-of-distribution test). The paper's own real-data result in Fig. 6 shows false-color artifacts inside the black-and-white pinwheel target for a three-measurement stack, which is precisely the kind of artifact the physics-based claim is meant to exclude.

Operational constraints limit practical utility and are only partially addressed: a 10° field of view (versus 32° for KRISM), a calibrated depth of field of roughly 34 cm at 2.64-2.98 m, and reliance on a specific PSF stack, with unmodeled spherical and lateral chromatic aberration acknowledged as residual model mismatch. The stated future work (extending working volume, reducing measurements for dynamic scenes) confirms these are unresolved limitations rather than edge cases.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: key hyperparameters (eigenspace dimension v, ADMM step sizes μ1/μ2, convergence thresholds), the identity of the off-the-shelf denoiser, and the calibration/optical details are deferred to a supplement that is not available for review, so the reported numbers cannot be independently verified from the paper alone.

strengths: Simple, genuinely low-cost optical design: two off-the-shelf lenses plus a grayscale sensor (4 optical components, vs. up to 20 for KRISM), avoiding coded apertures and dispersive elements, with a working hardware prototype and code/data promised publicly.

The reconstruction formulation is sensible and efficient: a PSF-based forward model y = CHx, PCA subspace projection onto natural-spectra eigenvectors, plug-and-play ADMM with a learned denoiser, and a BCCB fast-inversion formula yielding 0.64 s reconstruction on an RTX A6000 — a real computational advantage over SDC/Choi et al. (>15 min).

Real-data evaluation goes beyond a single demo: Macbeth color chart reconstruction with ΔE00 and SAM, plus robustness studies as a function of distance from the calibration plane and number of measurements (Figs. 4, 5), and qualitative lab scenes in Fig. 6.

The paper is reasonably clear about its physical assumptions and includes a comparison table (Table 1) that jointly reports reconstruction quality, compute time, FoV, and optical complexity — a useful framing for the community.
weaknesses: The headline state-of-the-art claim (Table 1, Fig. 3) rests entirely on simulation using the authors' own calibrated PSFs and their own Poisson noise model. There is no quantitative real-world comparison against any competing method; simulated evaluations implicitly assume the forward model is exact, which is precisely where chromatic-aberration systems break down in practice.

Baseline fairness is questionable. TF at -4.88 dB PSNR and Choi et al. at 15.97 dB with >15 min compute look under-tuned relative to their published results, and the comparison conflates different measurement counts, optics, and priors. The 'frame rate' metric 1/(t_exposure + t_compute) with a fixed 5 s exposure for every method is dominated by the assumed exposure and does not substantiate the 'fast/high frame rate' framing; the actual system still requires mechanically translating a lens and ≥5 measurements for clean output (Fig. 5b, Fig. 6), with visible false-color artifacts at 3 measurements.

Limited novelty. Chromatic focal sweep/stack for spectral reconstruction is well established (Cossairt & Nayar ICCP 2010 [10]; Huang et al. [17]; Zhan et al. [31]). The contribution essentially reduces to substituting a plug-and-play deep denoiser for a hand-crafted prior and adding PCA subspace projection — standard components — and the paper does not quantitatively compare against [10] or [17], only against the weak inverse-filtering baseline of Zhan et al.

Strong depth/calibration dependence is under-examined. The method assumes the target lies within a 34 cm depth of field around 2.8 m; PSFs are depth-dependent and defocus is ignored in the image formation model. Real experiments deliberately keep objects near the calibration plane, and sensitivity to PSF miscalibration, lens alignment error, or scene depth variation is never quantified.

Real-data accuracy is modest and its error metrics are not contextualized: per-patch SAM reaches 38.0° (Fig. 4) and mean ΔE00 = 3.77 exceeds the perceptual threshold of 2, which is dismissed as 'likely to go unnoticed in practice' with no user study or citation. The system recovers only 12 channels (400-694 nm), fewer than typical HSI benchmarks, and real-scene spectra are validated against reflectance references adjusted by the illuminant rather than true hyperspectral ground truth.

No ablation isolates the algorithmic contribution: the effect of the denoiser choice, the PCA dimension v, the ADMM iteration budget, and comparison against simpler priors are all missing. Only mean metrics over 30 Harvard images are reported, with no variance or per-image statistics, and no comparison to recent deep/transformer HSI methods beyond MST.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted version: key elements (denoiser architecture and training data, spectral response correction of the grayscale camera and filter, full PSF calibration procedure with 12 bandpass filters, ADMM derivations) are deferred to a supplement, and the code/data are only announced as forthcoming.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence: 'state-of-the-art spectral image quality,' 'fast computation,' and 'nearly all incident light' preservation are supported mainly by a self-referential simulation, while the abstract's '<1 second of compute' is a compute-only claim that does not translate into fast acquisition.

strengths: Simple and cost-effective optical design using two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor, eliminating the need for complex optics such as diffractive elements or spectral filters.
Fast reconstruction algorithm (0.64 s) leveraging plug-and-play ADMM with PCA-based spectral projection and BCCB-based fast matrix inversion, enabling sub-second processing.
State-of-the-art performance in simulation: best PSNR (30.81 dB) and SSIM (0.92), second-best SAM (7.35°) across three public datasets, with robustness to low exposure and noise demonstrated.
Real-world prototype validation shows feasibility, with reconstruction quality (29.54 dB PSNR, 7.42° SAM) matching simulation and detailed calibration and analysis.
Thorough ablation and robustness studies (e.g., effect of number of measurements, depth range, color checker performance) and acknowledged limitations provide a balanced view.
weaknesses: Lack of real-data comparison with other state-of-the-art methods; the SOTA claim relies solely on simulation, which may not fully capture real-world complexities and imperfections of competing modalities.
Algorithmic novelty is limited: plug-and-play ADMM, PCA-based spectral prior, and BCCB inversion are existing techniques combined for this specific application, with only modest modifications.

The use of chromatic aberration for spectral imaging is not entirely new (e.g., Zhan et al. [54]); the main novelty lies in the specific system design and fast reconstruction rather than the fundamental concept.

Capture requires five exposures with a moving lens, introducing mechanical delays and limiting dynamic scene applications; total acquisition time is not reported for the real prototype, and the 'fast' claim primarily applies to reconstruction, not capture.
The deep denoiser is off-the-shelf and pretrained on hyperspectral data; potential domain gap and its impact are only briefly discussed and relegated to the supplement.
Spatially invariant PSF assumption may not hold across the field, restricting the method to a narrow field of view (acknowledged) and potentially limiting practical applicability.

strengths: Proposes a novel chromatic focal stack system using only two off-the-shelf lenses, a grayscale sensor, and a moving lens, avoiding spectral filters, dispersers, or custom diffractive optics. This yields high photon efficiency and hardware simplicity compared to CASSI, diffuser-based, and DOE-based systems.

Provides a complete physics-based forward model with measured PSFs and a plug-and-play ADMM reconstruction algorithm, including a low-rank spectral prior and an off-the-shelf deep denoiser. The BCCB fast inversion enables sub-second reconstruction (0.64s), which is significantly faster than several baselines.

Reports strong simulation results on three public datasets (Harvard, KAIST, CAVE) against nine methods. It achieves the best PSNR (30.81 dB), ties best SSIM (0.92), and is second-best in SAM (7.35°), while using only 4 optical components and 0.64s compute time. This is competitive with MST and much simpler/faster than KRISM.

Includes a real-world prototype with calibration, measured PSFs, LCTF ground truth, Macbeth color checker, and real scenes. Real-data performance (PSNR 29.54 dB, SAM 7.42°) is close to simulation, demonstrating practical feasibility.

Analyzes robustness with respect to depth range and number of measurements, and shows a convincing low-exposure advantage over MST and KRISM in simulation, supporting the claimed photon-efficiency benefit.
The paper is generally well-written and structured, with clear figures, a useful comparison table, and promises of code/data release, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The 'fast' claim is only supported by reconstruction time; the system is not snapshot and requires translating a lens to five positions with a linear stage. Total capture/acquisition time, stage settling time, and suitability for dynamic scenes are not reported. Comparisons to snapshot methods use equal total exposure time but not equal total acquisition time, so the practical speed advantage is unclear.

The reconstruction is severely ill-posed (5 measurements for ~29–31 spectral bands) and relies heavily on a low-rank spectral basis derived from the Harvard dataset plus a learned denoiser. Generalization to spectra outside this prior is not ablated, and the main paper lacks details on the number of principal components and denoiser behavior. This limits claims of physical interpretability and hallucination mitigation.

Real-data validation is limited to a few scenes and a Macbeth chart and does not compare against competing modalities on real captures. The 'matches simulation' claim is therefore not supported against real-world baselines.

The optical model assumes spatially invariant PSFs and constant magnification. Field-dependent aberrations and calibration errors are not fully characterized, although the FOV is small. The acknowledged failure at 700 nm and in dark regions suggests remaining robustness issues.

The state-of-the-art claim is somewhat overstated: SSIM is tied with MST, SAM is second to KRISM, and the PSNR margin over MST is only 0.19 dB without error bars or statistical significance testing on the 30-image benchmark.

Baseline simulation may be unfair: methods like tunable filters and other modalities appear to perform much worse than in their original papers, and the same photon-budget/optical simulation may not fully reflect their optimized settings. This should be better justified.

The method criticizes data-driven hallucination but itself uses a learned denoiser and dataset-specific spectral prior. No quantitative hallucination metric is provided, only qualitative spectral curves, so the claimed robustness advantage over purely data-driven methods is not fully proven.

strengths: The optical design is genuinely simple and light-efficient: two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor, with no light-blocking filters or coded apertures, and the measured PSFs are incorporated directly into the forward model so that the encoding comes from naturally occurring chromatic aberration.

The hybrid reconstruction (plug-and-play ADMM with a spectral PCA prior and an off-the-shelf deep denoiser) is interpretable and fast, reporting sub-second reconstruction versus >15 minutes for iterative solvers such as KRISM.
A real hardware prototype is built and evaluated on real scenes (Fig. 4), not only in simulation, which is more than many computational-imaging papers provide.

The low-light advantage is a substantive and well-motivated result: SfD retains 27.59 dB PSNR where competing methods degrade to 14-20 dB (Fig. 3b), which follows directly from the photon-efficient, non-blocking design.
The simulation study is reasonably broad (three datasets, eight baselines) and is complemented by ablations on the number of measurements (Fig. 5a) and the working depth range (Fig. 5b).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. Chromatic-aberration / spectral focal-sweep imaging is established prior work (Zhan et al. [54], Cossairt & Nayar [13], He et al. [21], Huang et al. [26]), and every algorithmic ingredient (PnP-ADMM [53], spectral PCA prior [1], off-the-shelf denoiser [29]) is existing; the paper largely combines these, so the advance over Zhan et al. is a better algorithm rather than a new sensing principle.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim is marginal and not fully supported. PSNR is 30.81 vs. MST 30.62 (a negligible margin), SSIM is tied at 0.92, and KRISM attains a better SAM (6.91 vs. 7.35); the method is essentially tied, and this is under one specific 5-second simulation protocol.

Several baseline numbers are far below those reported in their original papers (e.g., Spectral DiffuserCam 15.59 dB, Spectral DefocusCam 21.17 dB, Choi et al. 23.97 dB) while MST matches published values. This inconsistency raises concerns about whether the re-implementations/training and the photon-budget equalization unfairly penalize certain modalities, which would undermine the central comparison.

The 'physics-based / interpretable / anti-hallucination' framing is overstated: the method depends on a learned denoiser and on a PCA prior derived from the Harvard dataset that is also used in evaluation, and hallucination robustness is asserted rather than quantified (e.g., on out-of-distribution scenes).

Real-data evaluation is narrow and the ground truth is approximate: reference images are captured with an LCTF that has finite bandwidth and its own spectral errors, only a few scenes are shown, some exhibit weak SAM (up to 24.3°), and the usable field is a ~40% sensor crop with a 9.7° FOV and only a 34 cm working range.

With only N=5 measurements reconstructing tens of spectral channels, the spectra are visibly oversmoothed (as the authors admit) and spectral resolution is inherently limited; the number of channels C actually reconstructed in simulation versus on real data is not clearly specified, making the spectral-fidelity claims hard to assess.
Minor presentation issues, e.g., Table 1 labels Spectral DiffuserCam as a 'Spectral Filter' modality (it is lensless) and some optical-component counts/categories appear inconsistent.
